It is the case of the petitioner that on 19.03.2013 she reached DTC Bus Stand at Rajender Nagar crossing and while she was crossing the road one car bearing No.DL4CAF8777 came at very fast speed and hit the deceased (ought to be petitioner) with very great force. It is averred that due to the forceful impact the injured fell down on the road and sustained grievous injuries. It is averred that the accident occurred due to the rash and negligent driving, in contravention of the traffic rules by the driver who was driving the offending vehicle. It is stated that the driver of the offending vehicle Ms. Neetu Kushwaha vs Shri Brij Mohan Shah on 28 October, 2014 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/113545340/ 1 took the injured to Sir Ganga Ram Hospital after the accident and the MLC of the petitioner was prepared and the injuries sustained were grievous in nature. In respect of the accident FIR bearing No.50/13 under Sections 279/338 IPC was registered at PS Inder Puri. It is averred that the accident occurred due to the rash and negligent driving of the respondent No.1 and an innocent person Neetu Kushwah v Brij Mohan Shah & Ors. Page No. 2 of 29 became the victim of the same. It is averred that at the time of the accident the respondent No.1 was the driver, the respondent No.2 was the owner and the respondent No.3 was the insurance company of the said vehicle so all the respondents are jointly and severally liable to pay compensation amount to the petitioner. 3. It is averred that the petitioner was 18 years old and was doing a private job. It is stated that the petitioner is a student of CS and simultaneously part time working to carry on her studies. It is stated that the petitioner is a bright student with a brilliant academic record and due to the accident she suffered loss of studies. It is stated that the petitioner was admitted in Sir Ganga Ram hospital where MLC was prepared and later her treatment was carried on from ESI Hospital, Safdarjung and she was still under treatment. It is averred that Rs.1,00,000/ approximately were spent on treatment. It is prayed that an amount of Rs.6,00,000/ be awarded as compensation in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents. 4. Reply was filed to the DAR on behalf of the respondents No.1 and 2 averring that the DAR had been filed by the police on false and frivolous ground by concocting a false story of accident at the instance of the complainant. Page No. 3 of 29 driver at the alleged date, time and place of accident in the manner stated in the DAR. Thereafter written statement was filed on behalf of the respondents No.1 and 2 taking the preliminary objections that the petition has been filed without any cause of action with malafide intention and just to harass and grab the money from the respondents. It is averred that the vehicle in question was not present at the time and place of occurrence as alleged and the said vehicle had been falsely implicated at the instance of the complainant and thereafter the police officials of the concerned police station had registered a false FIR against the respondents No.1 and 2. The averments made in the claim petition were denied. It is averred that the petitioner has not mentioned in her petition from where and how she is/ was earning Rs.10,000/ per month. It is averred that the vehicle was planted in the matter and no accident was caused by the vehicle as well as by the respondent No.1 (driver). It is averred that the amount of Rs.1,00,000/ approximately appears to be unreal and exaggerated and without any documentary proof. It is averred that the vehicle in question i.e. DL 4CAF8777 Ford Fiesta was duly insured with the respondent No.3 on the day of the alleged occurrence/ accident and the respondent No.1 was also holding effective and valid driving license at that time. 5. She stated that the family of the petitioner is a poor family and they could not afford the expensive hospital, therefore, at a later stage her treatment was carried on from ESI Hospital and Safdarjung. She stated that she was doing a private job in Society for Education and Economic Development and earning Rs.8,500/ per month. She left her job in the month of January, 2013 due to some personal difficulties and she was given standing offer to rejoin the organization and she was about to rejoin her duty on 20.3.2013 but due to the accident she could not rejoin her duty. She stated that after the accident she was not in a position to rejoin her duty. She stated that she is a good academic student and she wants to keep her study Neetu Kushwah v Brij Mohan Shah & Ors. Page No. 7 of 29 on after the job, as she was bearing her own expenses of her study but due to the accident she could not study further as she was not in a position to walk or even talk properly. Page No. 15 of 29 others (2002) 6 SCC 455 where it was observed: "The following observation of the High Court of Australia in Astley v. Austrust Ltd. ((1999) 73 ALJR 403) is worthy of quoting. A finding of contributory negligence turns on a factual investigation whether the plaintiff contributed to his or her own loss by failing to take reasonable care of his or her person or property. What is reasonable care depends on the circumstances of the case. In many cases, it may be proper for a plaintiff to rely on the defendant to perform its duty. But there is no absolute rule. The duties and responsibilities of the defendant are a variable factor in determining whether contributory negligence exists and, if so, to what degree. In some cases, the nature of the duty owed may exculpate the plaintiff from a claim of contributory negligence; in other cases, the nature of the duty may reduce the plaintiff's share of responsibility for the damage suffered; and in yet other cases the nature of the duty may not prevent a finding that the plaintiff failed to take reasonable care for the safety of his or her person or property. The duty owed by the defendant, although relevant, is one only of many factors that must be weighed in determining whether the plaintiff has so conducted itself that it failed to take reasonable care for the safety of its person or property." In this case the contributory negligence of the claimant was held to be 25%. Further the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in Leela Bai v. The Managing Director & Ors. decided on 13.6.2012 held the contributory negligence of the deceased who was attempting to cross the road on the flyover to be 40%. Where a person is injured as a result of negligence on the part of two or more wrongdoers, it is said that the person was injured on account of the composite negligence of those wrongdoers. In such a case, each wrongdoer is jointly and severally liable to the injured for payment of the entire damages and the injured person has the choice of proceeding against all or any of them. Where the injured is guilty of some negligence, his claim for damages is not defeated merely by reason of the negligence on his part but the damages recoverable by him in respect of the injuries stands reduced in proportion to his contributory negligence." Thus the petitioner would have been more than 22 years old on the date of the accident i.e. 19.3.2013. texts.other_lawyer_arguments: It is established law that in a claim petition under Motor Vehicle Act, the standard of proof to establish rash and negligent driving by the driver of the offending vehicle is not at par with the criminal case where such rashness and negligence is required to be proved beyond all shadow of reasonable Neetu Kushwah v Brij Mohan Shah & Ors. Page No. 9 of 29 doubt. In Kaushnamma Begum and others v. New India Assurance Company Limited, it was inter alia held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that the issue of wrongful act or omission on the part of the driver of the motor vehicle involved in the accident has been left to a secondary importance and mere use or involvement of motor vehicle in causing bodily injury or death to a human being or damage to property would make the petition maintainable under Sections 166 and 140 of the Motor Vehicle Act. It was averred that due to the forceful impact the injured fell down on the road and sustained grievous injuries. In Basant Kaur and others v. Chattar Pal Singh and others 2003 ACJ 369 MP (DB) it was observed that registration of criminal case against the driver of the offending vehicle was enough to record a finding that the driver of the offending vehicle was responsible for causing the accident. In view of the testimony of PW1 Neetu Kushwah v Brij Mohan Shah & Ors. Page No. 14 of 29 and documents on record which have remained unrebutted, the negligence of respondent No.1 has been prima facie proved. The Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in Koosappa Poojari v. K. Sadabba & Ors. MFA No.6208 of 2002 decided on 21.11.2003 observed that the driver of the vehicle ought to have been more prudent and circumspect while driving. It was however also observed: "But it cannot be lost sight of the fact that a duty is also cast on a pedestrian and he should use due care and caution in going upon and crossing the road and it is his duty to look out for on coming traffic. It is not always necessary that the vehicular traffic will have to stop for a pedestrian to cross, for the vehicle needs more time to stop in view of the speed a motor generates. Moreover, whenever a pedestrian is crossing over a roadway at any place other than which is meant for pedestrian crossing, they cannot claim any specific precedence and the responsibility for causing the accident more often than not will have to be shared by the pedestrian along with the vehicle driver. Reliance was placed in this judgment on the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Pramodkumar Rasikbhai Jhaveri v. Karmasey Kunvargi Tak and Neetu Kushwah v Brij Mohan Shah Ms. Neetu Kushwaha vs Shri Brij Mohan Shah on 28 October, 2014 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/113545340/ 7 & Ors. Page No. 15 of 29 others (2002) 6 SCC 455 where it was observed: "The following observation of the High Court of Australia in Astley v. Austrust Ltd. ((1999) 73 ALJR 403) is worthy of quoting. A finding of contributory negligence turns on a factual investigation whether the plaintiff contributed to his or her own loss by failing to take reasonable care of his or her person or property. What is reasonable care depends on the circumstances of the case. In many cases, it may be proper for a plaintiff to rely on the defendant to perform its duty. But there is no absolute rule. The duties and responsibilities of the defendant are a variable factor in determining whether contributory negligence exists and, if so, to what degree. In some cases, the nature of the duty owed may exculpate the plaintiff from a claim of contributory negligence; in other cases, the nature of the duty may reduce the plaintiff's share of responsibility for the damage suffered; and in yet other cases the nature of the duty may not prevent a finding that the plaintiff failed to take reasonable care for the safety of his or her person or property. The duty owed by the defendant, although relevant, is one only of many factors that must be weighed in determining whether the plaintiff has so conducted itself that it failed to take reasonable care for the safety of its person or property." In this case the contributory negligence of the claimant was held to be 25%. Further the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in Leela Bai v. The Managing Director & Ors. decided on 13.6.2012 held the contributory negligence of the deceased who was attempting to cross the road on the flyover to be 40%. Page No. 16 of 29 apportioned as 25% and the negligence of the respondent No.1 would be 75%. 'Composite negligence' refers to the negligence on the part of two or more persons. Where a person is injured as a result of negligence on the part of two or more wrongdoers, it is said that the person was injured on account of the composite negligence of those wrongdoers. In such a case, each wrongdoer is jointly and severally liable to the injured for payment of the entire damages and the injured person has the choice of proceeding against all or any of them. In such a case, the Ms. Neetu Kushwaha vs Shri Brij Mohan Shah on 28 October, 2014 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/113545340/ 8 injured need not establish the extent of responsibility of each wrongdoer separately, nor is it necessary for Neetu Kushwah v Brij Mohan Shah & Ors. Page No. 17 of 29 the court to determine the extent of liability of each wrongdoer separately. Where the injured is guilty of some negligence, his claim for damages is not defeated merely by reason of the negligence on his part but the damages recoverable by him in respect of the injuries stands reduced in proportion to his contributory negligence." In addition, the injured is further entitled to nonpecuniary damages/general damages which include (1) damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of injuries and (2) loss of expectation of life. Neetu Kushwah v Brij Mohan Shah & Ors. It has been held in Divisional Controller, K. S. R. T. C v Mahadeva Shetty and another AIR 2003 Supreme Court 4172 as under: 13."The damages for vehicular accidents are in the nature of compensation in money for less of any kind caused to any person. In Parry V. Cleaver (1969 1 All. E. R. 555) Lord Morris stated as follows: "To compensate in money for pain and for the physical consequences is invariably difficult, but no other process can be devised than that of making monetary assessment."
